tomato_early_blight.name: Tomato Early Blight
symptoms: Dark brown circular spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on lower leaves
Yellow halo surrounding the brown lesions
Lesions merge causing large blighted areas; severely affected leaves turn yellow and drop
Stem lesions appear as dark, slightly sunken areas near soil line in seedlings (collar rot)
tomato_early_blight.explanation: The distinctive concentric ring pattern on older leaves is the key visual cue — it mimics a target or bull's-eye, caused by the fungus Alternaria solani expanding outward as it kills host tissue. Infections typically start on the most mature (lowest) leaves, which is another diagnostic indicator.

steps: Remove and destroy all visibly infected leaves immediately — do not compost them
Apply neem oil spray (2% concentration — 20ml per litre of water with a few drops of liquid soap as emulsifier) every 7–10 days, starting before symptoms are widespread
Alternatively, spray copper-based Bordeaux mixture (1% concentration) as an organic fungicide
Mulch around the base of plants to prevent soil splash, which spreads fungal spores upward
Water at the base of the plant (drip or furrow), not overhead, to keep foliage dry
preventiveTips: Use certified disease-free seeds or resistant varieties (e.g., Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat)
Follow crop rotation — do not grow tomato, potato, or other Solanaceae in the same plot for at least 2–3 seasons
Maintain adequate plant spacing (45–60 cm) for air circulation to reduce humidity around leaves
Apply potassium-rich fertilizer to strengthen plant cell walls against fungal penetration
Scout fields weekly from transplanting; early intervention prevents rapid spread

tomato_late_blight.name: Tomato Late Blight
symptoms: Pale green to brown water-soaked patches on leaf margins and tips, rapidly darkening
White cottony mold visible on leaf undersides in humid conditions (early morning)
Stem turns dark brown/black; infected fruit shows firm, brown, greasy-looking lesions
Entire plant can collapse within days in warm, wet weather
tomato_late_blight.explanation: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) progresses far faster than early blight — the water-soaked, greasy appearance of lesions and white sporulation on the leaf underside distinguish it. It requires wet, cool conditions (15–22°C) to spread, and a single infected plant can devastate a field rapidly.

steps: Act immediately — late blight spreads extremely rapidly; delay of 24–48 hours can mean losing an entire field
Remove and bag (do not compost) all heavily infected plants or branches; dispose away from the field
Apply copper hydroxide or copper oxychloride spray (0.3% — 3g per litre) covering both leaf surfaces thoroughly
Spray Trichoderma viride biological fungicide (4–5g per litre) as an organic alternative or supplement
Repeat sprays every 5–7 days while wet conditions persist
preventiveTips: Plant resistant varieties — check with your local KVK for varieties suited to your region
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to keep foliage dry
Ensure good air drainage — avoid low-lying, poorly ventilated plots for tomato cultivation
Scout daily during monsoon season and after cool, rainy spells when risk is highest
Do not store seed from infected plants

rice_blast.name: Rice Blast
symptoms: Diamond or eye-shaped lesions with grey centres and brown borders on leaves
Neck rot — dark brown discolouration at the base of the panicle causing 'dead heart' or empty grains
Lesions may be pale grey with dark borders on susceptible varieties; smaller reddish-brown on resistant varieties
Severely infected seedlings die completely (seedling blight stage)
rice_blast.explanation: The diamond-shaped ('eye-shaped') lesion with a grey centre is the classic diagnostic feature of rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae). Neck blast — infection at the panicle base — is the most economically destructive stage because it causes total grain loss even when leaves appear relatively healthy.

steps: Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens biological agent (10g per litre) as a preventive and early curative measure
Apply Trichoderma harzianum (5g per litre) as a soil drench around roots at transplanting and tillering
For foliar treatment, spray neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) at 5% concentration every 10 days
Remove and bury infected stubble after harvest — do not leave on field surface
Drain and dry fields periodically (intermittent drainage) to reduce humidity near the canopy
preventiveTips: Use blast-resistant varieties certified by your state agricultural university for your agro-climatic zone
Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride (4g per kg seed) before sowing
Avoid excess nitrogen application — high nitrogen makes plants lush and more susceptible to blast
Maintain optimum plant spacing to improve air circulation
Monitor fields weekly, especially during flowering which is the most vulnerable stage for neck blast

wheat_stem_rust.name: Wheat Stem Rust
symptoms: Reddish-brown to brick-red oval pustules (uredinia) on stems and leaf sheaths, easily rubbing off as rust powder
Pustules can also appear on leaf blades and glumes
Infected tissue collapses; severe infections cause lodging (stems fall over) and shrivelled grains
Black pustules (telia) appear at crop maturity — dark sooty streaks on stems and sheaths
wheat_stem_rust.explanation: The brick-red, powder-releasing pustules on the stem are unmistakable — rust-coloured powder rubbing onto your finger confirms Puccinia graminis infection. Stem rust spreads very rapidly via airborne spores and can cause 70–100% yield loss in susceptible varieties if conditions are favourable (warm, humid weather 15–25°C).

steps: If detected early, apply sulphur-based wettable powder (80% WP, 2g per litre) as an organic-compatible fungicide spray
Spray neem oil (3ml per litre) as a supplementary treatment — repeat every 7 days
Destroy heavily infected crop residues after harvest by deep burial or burning (check local regulations on burning)
Report confirmed Ug99 or new-race detections to the nearest KVK or state agricultural department immediately
preventiveTips: Grow certified rust-resistant varieties — this is the single most effective preventive measure
Sow on the recommended date for your region — delayed sowing increases rust risk
Avoid excessive nitrogen application which promotes lush, susceptible growth
Remove volunteer wheat plants and alternative hosts (barberry, Berberis spp.) near fields
Monitor fields from booting stage onward when rust risk peaks

maize_northern_leaf_blight.name: Maize Northern Leaf Blight
symptoms: Long (5–15 cm), cigar-shaped greyish-green to tan lesions with wavy, irregular margins on leaves
Lesions typically start on lower leaves and progress upward
Under humid conditions, dark grey-green sporulation visible in the lesion centre
Severe infections cause leaves to appear completely blighted and scorched
maize_northern_leaf_blight.explanation: The elongated, cigar-shaped lesion is the key identifier for Northern Leaf Blight (Exserohilum turcicum). Unlike other leaf diseases that cause circular or angular spots, NLB lesions run parallel to the leaf veins and can reach 15 cm in length. Losses are highest when infection reaches the ear leaf before tasseling.

steps: Spray neem oil (2% concentration) every 10 days from first symptom appearance
Apply Trichoderma viride biological agent (5g per litre) as foliar spray
Remove and destroy heavily infected lower leaves to slow upward spread
Avoid overhead irrigation; use furrow or drip irrigation
preventiveTips: Plant resistant hybrids — consult your seed supplier for NLB-resistant varieties suited to your region
Practice crop rotation — maize-legume rotation breaks the disease cycle
Plough under crop residues after harvest to reduce inoculum for the next season
Ensure adequate plant spacing for air circulation
Avoid water stress which weakens plant defenses

cotton_leaf_curl.name: Cotton Leaf Curl Disease
symptoms: Upward or downward curling and cupping of leaves — the most distinctive symptom
Thickened veins and leaf veins turning dark green or purple (vein swelling)
Small leaf-like outgrowths (enations) on the underside of leaves
Stunted plant growth; severe infections prevent boll formation
cotton_leaf_curl.explanation: Cotton Leaf Curl is caused by a Begomovirus transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). The upward curling of leaves with thickened veins and enations on the underside is unmistakable. Unlike fungal diseases, this is viral — there is no chemical cure; management focuses entirely on controlling the whitefly vector and removing infected plants.

steps: Remove and destroy severely infected plants immediately to reduce the viral reservoir
Control whitefly population using yellow sticky traps (1 trap per 25 plants)
Spray neem oil (5ml per litre) every 7 days to repel and reduce whitefly numbers
Apply reflective mulch (silver/aluminium) between rows — whiteflies avoid reflected light
Spray soap solution (5g liquid soap per litre) on leaf undersides where whiteflies congregate
preventiveTips: Use certified CLCuD-tolerant varieties — check with your KVK for recommended varieties
Avoid planting near fields with previous CLCuD infection history
Plant maize or sorghum border crops — they act as windbreaks reducing whitefly migration
Plant on recommended dates — avoid early or late sowing which coincides with peak whitefly populations
Do not leave infected crop debris in the field after harvest

potato_late_blight.name: Potato Late Blight
symptoms: Pale green water-soaked patches on leaf tips and margins turning dark brown rapidly
White sporulation on the underside of infected leaves in cool, humid mornings
Infected tubers show brown, firm, dry rot extending inward from the skin
Entire foliage can collapse within 3–7 days in cool, wet weather
potato_late_blight.explanation: Potato late blight (Phytophthora infestans — the same pathogen as tomato late blight) famously caused the Irish Famine. The white mold visible on leaf undersides in humid conditions is diagnostic. Tuber infection is particularly damaging because infected tubers continue to rot in storage.

steps: Act within 24 hours of first symptom appearance — late blight is one of the fastest-spreading plant diseases
Remove and destroy infected foliage; hill up soil around plants to protect tubers from spores washing down
Spray copper oxychloride (0.3%) or Bordeaux mixture (1%) covering all leaf surfaces
Apply Trichoderma-based biological fungicide as a soil drench to protect tubers
Stop irrigating immediately — withhold water to reduce humidity
preventiveTips: Use certified disease-free seed tubers — never plant tubers from a diseased field
Plant resistant varieties appropriate for your region
Store seed tubers in well-ventilated, cool, dry conditions before planting
Avoid overcast, rainy season planting if possible
Scout fields daily during cool, cloudy weather — this is when late blight strikes

chilli_anthracnose.name: Chilli Anthracnose (Fruit Rot)
symptoms: Circular, sunken, water-soaked lesions on ripening and ripe fruit — often tan or brown with orange-pink spore masses in the centre
Infected fruit shrivels, darkens, and mummifies on the plant
Leaf and stem lesions are less common but appear as dark, slightly sunken spots
Post-harvest fruit rot continues in storage
chilli_anthracnose.explanation: Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.) primarily attacks ripening fruit — the sunken, water-soaked lesion with salmon-pink spore masses in the centre is the defining feature. The disease can cause 50–80% post-harvest losses if harvested fruit carries latent infection. Hot, humid conditions favour rapid spread.

steps: Harvest fruit promptly at the right maturity — overripe fruit is most susceptible
Remove and destroy mummified infected fruit on the plant and on the ground
Spray neem oil (2%) or copper-based fungicide every 10 days during fruit development
Apply Trichoderma viride as a soil drench to reduce soilborne inoculum
Handle harvested fruit carefully — wounds are entry points for the pathogen
preventiveTips: Use certified disease-free seeds; treat seeds with hot water (50°C for 30 minutes) before sowing
Practice crop rotation — avoid chilli after chilli
Maintain plant spacing for good air circulation to reduce humidity
Avoid overhead irrigation especially during fruiting stage
Store harvested fruit in cool, well-ventilated conditions immediately after harvest

groundnut_early_leaf_spot.name: Groundnut Early Leaf Spot
symptoms: Circular, dark brown spots (3–10 mm) with yellow halos on the upper leaf surface
Spots appear darker brown on upper surface, lighter on lower surface (distinguishes it from late leaf spot which is darker below)
Spots start on older leaves and progress upward
Severe defoliation begins from lower leaves in heavy infections
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.explanation: Early leaf spot (Cercospora arachidicola) is distinguished from late leaf spot by the darker colour of lesions on the upper leaf surface compared to the lower surface. The yellow halo around the lesion is more pronounced than in late leaf spot. Losses of 50% are possible in susceptible varieties with no management.

steps: Spray neem leaf extract (5% — boil and strain 500g neem leaves per 10 litres water) every 10–14 days
Apply sulphur dust or wettable sulphur spray (2g per litre) as an organic fungicide option
Remove and bury or compost infected fallen leaves
Spray Trichoderma viride (5g per litre) as a biological management option
preventiveTips: Grow resistant varieties — consult your local KVK for varieties adapted to your region
Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride (4g per kg) before sowing
Avoid plant stress through timely irrigation, especially during pod filling
Practice crop rotation — cereals or pulses make good rotational crops
Scout fields from 30 days after sowing — early intervention matters

sugarcane_red_rot.name: Sugarcane Red Rot
symptoms: Leaves of the top shoot (crown leaves) wither and dry from the tip downward
Cutting the stalk longitudinally reveals reddish discolouration of internal tissue with white patches at intervals — the most diagnostic feature
A sour, alcoholic smell from infected stalks due to fermentation of sugar content
Infected stools die prematurely; gaps visible in the field
sugarcane_red_rot.explanation: Red rot (Colletotrichum falcatum) is the most destructive sugarcane disease in India. The internal red discolouration with white spots inside the stalk is pathognomonic — no other disease causes this exact pattern. The alcoholic smell from infected cane is another reliable on-field indicator. Disease spreads through infected seed sets and waterlogging.

steps: Rogue out and remove all infected stools immediately — uproot completely, do not just cut
Drench the soil around removed plants with copper oxychloride solution (0.3%) to reduce soilborne spread
Treat remaining healthy plants with Trichoderma viride soil drench
Improve field drainage immediately — waterlogging greatly accelerates spread
Do not use infected stalks as seed material under any circumstances
preventiveTips: Use certified disease-free seed sets from healthy stools
Treat seed sets before planting: soak in Carbendazim (0.1%) or Trichoderma viride solution for 30 minutes
Plant resistant/tolerant varieties — Co 86032, CoC 671, Co 0238 are known for better tolerance in many regions
Ensure good field drainage — avoid low-lying waterlogged plots for sugarcane
Avoid using cutting tools between healthy and potentially infected fields without cleaning/disinfecting
